n: Zechariah began prophesying in late 520 BC, just two months after Haggai, to the Jews rebuilding the temple. He was from a priestly family that returned from Babylon.
The Lord was very angry with their ancestors, whose sins led to Jerusalem’s destruction and exile.
The key invitation of the book: “Turn to Me, and I will turn to you.” God is ready to meet anyone who comes back to Him.

f.w: Turn ye unto me, saith the LORD of hosts, and I will turn unto you

n: Don’t be like your ancestors who ignored the earlier prophets’ calls to repent.

f.g: Prophets before the exile, such as Isaiah and Jeremiah.

f.w: Turn ye now from your evil ways

n: Where are your ancestors now? And the prophets — they didn’t live forever either. People pass away; God’s word remains.
God’s words caught up with their ancestors, who finally admitted, “The Lord dealt with us just as our ways deserved.” Prophecy proves true.

f.g: Overtake — like a pursuer catching up.

n: Three months later (February 519 BC), Zechariah receives a series of eight night visions.
Vision one: a man on a red horse stands among myrtle trees in a hollow, with red, sorrel, and white horses behind him.

f.g: Fragrant evergreen shrubs; later a symbol of Israel’s restoration (Isaiah 55:13).

n: Zechariah asks what they mean. An interpreting angel promises to explain — a pattern throughout these visions.

f.w: the angel that talked with me
f.g: A guiding angel who explains each vision.

n: The rider explains: these are the Lord’s scouts, sent to patrol the earth.

f.w: walk to and fro through the earth

n: The patrol reports to the angel of the Lord: the whole earth is calm and at rest. The Persian Empire was at peace — yet Jerusalem remained in ruins.

f.g: A heavenly messenger who speaks with God’s authority.

n: The angel of the Lord intercedes: “How long, Lord, before You show mercy to Jerusalem? You’ve been angry for seventy years.” Heaven itself pleads for God’s people.
The Lord replies with kind and comforting words.
The message to proclaim: the Lord is deeply, passionately devoted to Jerusalem and Zion.
God is angry with nations that feel secure. He was only a little angry with His people, but those nations went too far in hurting them.

f.g: They made the punishment worse than God intended.

f.w: I was but a little displeased

n: The Lord has returned to Jerusalem with mercy. His temple will be rebuilt and the city measured out again for rebuilding.

f.w: my house shall be built in it
a line shall be stretched forth
f.g: A measuring line — a sign of planned rebuilding.

n: God’s cities will overflow with prosperity again. He will comfort Zion and choose Jerusalem.

f.w: the LORD shall yet comfort Zion

n: Vision two: Zechariah sees four horns. In scripture, horns symbolize power, especially of kings and nations.

f.g: Four could represent the four directions — every power from all sides.

n: The angel explains: these horns are the powers that scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem.
Then the Lord shows four craftsmen.

f.g: Craftsmen or smiths — workers skilled in shaping and breaking.

n: The craftsmen have come to terrify and cut down the horns. For every power that harms God’s people, God has an answer.

f.w: cast out the horns of the Gentiles
